\chapter{Numbers Six to Ten}
\label{ch:hi-numbers-six-to-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from six to ten in Hindi and hear the sound changes that wore the Sanskrit numerals down.}

Trace ṣaṣ $\to$ chhah, nava $\to$ nau and daśa $\to$ das, naming the one change each numeral underwent.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[chha]{\hi{छ} — the puff again, on a letter you already have}

\label{lesson:HI-S130-letter-chha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \textbf{\hi{च}} — what sound does it carry?

You have met this arrangement once before, with \textbf{\hi{त}} and \textbf{\hi{थ}}. It is about to happen again.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{छ}}
\textbf{\hi{छ}} — \emph{chha}.

It is the \textbf{breathy partner of \hi{च}}, exactly as \textbf{\hi{थ}} is the breathy partner of \textbf{\hi{त}}. Say \emph{cha}, then say it again with a puff of air behind it, and you have the difference.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a continuous upper-left loop, lower bowl, outer-right rise and inner loop
  \item a short upper stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script: the pattern, a second time}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{character} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{puff of breath} \\
\midrule
\hi{च} & ca & no \\
\hi{छ} & chha & yes \\
\hi{त} & ta & no \\
\hi{थ} & tha & yes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four characters, two pairs, one distinction running through both. \textbf{This script pairs its letters by breath}, and once you have heard the pair once you can expect it everywhere — there are more pairs waiting, and each will cost you less than the last.

Unlike \textbf{\hi{त}} and \textbf{\hi{थ}}, the two shapes here look nothing alike. The sound is paired; the drawing is not.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{छ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the upper loop's open right tip, sweep counterclockwise around the upper-left loop, continue clockwise around the broad lower bowl, rise along the outer right side, and curl counterclockwise around the inner loop to its down-right tip without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the short upper stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified three-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline; everyday handwriting may divide or simplify the loops differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{छ}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \hi{च} and \hi{छ} side by side, and say which one carries the puff
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{च}  ·  \hi{छ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{छ} three times, saying \emph{chha} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} the other pair in this script that works the same way
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is \textbf{\hi{छ}} the breathy partner of? (\textbf{\hi{च}}.) Which earlier pair works the same way? (\textbf{\hi{त}} and \textbf{\hi{थ}}.) Do the two shapes resemble each other? (No — the sound is paired, the drawing is not.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chhah sāt āṭh nau das]{\hi{छह}, \hi{सात}, \hi{आठ}, \hi{नौ}, \hi{दस} — six to ten, the same erosion twice more}

\label{lesson:HI-C21-numbers-6-10}



\begin{quote}
You already watched \emph{trīṇi} wear down to \emph{tīn} in two careful steps. Two more numbers here do exactly the same thing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The five}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
6 & \textbf{\hi{छह}} & \emph{chhah} \\
7 & \textbf{\hi{सात}} & \emph{sāt} \\
8 & \textbf{\hi{आठ}} & \emph{āṭh} \\
9 & \textbf{\hi{नौ}} & \emph{nau} \\
10 & \textbf{\hi{दस}} & \emph{das} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — sapta $\to$ satta $\to$ sāt, aṣṭa $\to$ aṭṭha $\to$ āṭh — the same mechanism again}
Put seven and eight beside their Sanskrit ancestors:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{$\to$ Prakrit $\to$} & \textbf{Hindi} \\
\midrule
\emph{saptá} & \emph{satta} & \textbf{sāt} \\
\emph{aṣṭá} & \emph{aṭṭha} & \textbf{āṭh} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This is the \textbf{identical two-step process} you already watched turn \emph{trīṇi} into \emph{tīn}:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item The consonant cluster (\emph{-pt-}, \emph{-ṣṭ-}) \textbf{simplifies into a doubled consonant} (\emph{-tt-}, \emph{-ṭṭh-}) — the same weight, packed into one place.
  \item The doubled consonant \textbf{simplifies again}, and the \textbf{vowel lengthens} to pay for what was lost — \emph{satta} $\to$ \emph{sāt}, \emph{aṭṭha} $\to$ \emph{āṭh}.
\end{enumerate}

Same trade, same reason, two more numbers. This is exactly what the anchor lesson meant by \textquotedblleft{}not decay in any bad sense\textquotedblright{} — it's the standard Prakrit weight-conservation move, and by now you've seen it three times.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}chhah, sāt, āṭh, nau, das\textquotedblright{}
  \item the repeated mechanism — \textquotedblleft{}saptá … satta … \textbf{sāt}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}aṣṭá … aṭṭha … \textbf{āṭh}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count six to ten in Hindi. (\emph{Chhah, sāt, āṭh, nau, das}.) What mechanism do \emph{sāt} and \emph{āṭh} share with lesson 6's \emph{tīn}? (\textbf{Cluster simplifies to a geminate, then the geminate simplifies again and the vowel lengthens} — the same weight-conservation move, three numbers running.) Next: compare the three different histories inside six, nine, and ten.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chhah, nau, das]{\hi{छह}, \hi{नौ}, \hi{दस} — three different paths}

\label{lesson:HI-C21-six-nine-ten-history}



\begin{quote}
Seven and eight repeated a familiar weight trade. Six, nine, and ten show that not every number took the same road.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — ṣaṣ $\to$ chhah — a sibilant moves forward}
\textbf{\hi{छह}} (\emph{chhah}) continues Sanskrit \textbf{ṣaṣ}, \textquotedblleft{}six.\textquotedblright{} The retroflex sibilant \textbf{ṣ} shifted forward into Hindi \textbf{\hi{छ}} (\emph{ch}). This is separate from cluster simplification, but it is still two thousand years of ordinary speech reshaping a Sanskrit word.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — nava $\to$ nau — a consonant dissolves}
\textbf{\hi{नौ}} (\emph{nau}) continues Sanskrit \textbf{nava}. The \textbf{v} between vowels weakened and disappeared; the vowels on either side contracted into the diphthong \emph{-ava-} $\to$ \emph{-au-}. Compare \emph{pāṁch}: there a nasal moved into the vowel; here an intervocalic consonant dissolved between two vowels.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — daśa $\to$ das — the quiet path}
\textbf{\hi{दस}} (\emph{das}) continues Sanskrit \textbf{daśa} most plainly: the final vowel drops. There is no cluster to simplify and no middle consonant to lose.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ṣaṣ … chhah\textquotedblright{} — the sibilant shifts
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nava … nau\textquotedblright{} — \emph{v} dissolves into a diphthong
  \item \textquotedblleft{}daśa … das\textquotedblright{} — only the final vowel drops
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happened to \textbf{v} in \emph{nava} $\to$ \emph{nau}? (It \textbf{dissolved between vowels}, which contracted.) Which form changed least? (\textbf{Das} — only the final vowel dropped.) Count six to ten once more. (\emph{Chhah, sāt, āṭh, nau, das}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
